newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator says making progress on tax cut bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator says making progress on tax cut bill.

text.p: The chairman of the House-Senate group trying to craft a final tax cut bill said progress was made during a meeting Wednesday evening with White House officials.

"There was a very candid positive discussion of the issues, we're working hard to get a tax package through ... and we hope that we will be able to do it in the relatively near future," said Sen. William Roth, a Delaware Republican who chairs the House-Senate conference on the tax bill.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles attended the two-hour meeting, but would not comment on it afterward, deferring to Roth.
Roth said major items such as a capital gains tax cut, a $500 per child tax credit, and a proposed cigarette tax increase were discussed.
"We're united in wanting to get a tax package through," Roth said. "I would say we made progress."
The group of House and Senate lawmakers are trying to work out differences between their separate bills and put together one final tax cut package, while taking White House views into consideration.
Senate tax negotiators planned to send a first counteroffer to the House group, which in its first offer yielded to the Senate on some relatively minor issues.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, earlier Wednesday met with some Republican members of his committee and House Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas. Archer said there was "a lot of sensitivity" that the final bill should be a net $85 billion tax cut over five years.
Archer said an analysis of President Clinton's tax plan showed it fell far short of that goal set in the May budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House.
White House Budget Director Franklin Raines said Clinton's plan did result in an $85 billion net tax cut.
Archer said Clinton's tax plan would amount to a $56.8 billion tax cut over five years partly due to a proposed 20-cents per pack cigarette tax increase.
The tobacco tax increase would raise about $15 billion over five years. It is also included in the Senate tax bill and pulled the net tax cut in that version down to $77 billion over five years.
A "significant number" of House members did not support the cigarette tax increase, Archer said.
